title: Research Bite #10: Engaging “Silent” Students in Classroom Discussions
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #10 covers Morek, Heller, and Kinalzik's micro-analytic study of how teachers actually enact cold-calling in German middle-school classrooms, examining not whether cold-calling works but how the fine-grained way it is delivered shapes whether students experience it as engaging or threatening. The authors break cold-calling into a three-part sequence — a preparation phase that sets up the participation framework, the direct address and task itself, and a post-phase where the student responds and the teacher reacts — and analyze how verbal choices and embodied cues (posture, gaze, facial expression, gesture) shape each phase. Comparing two contrasting cases, the study finds that framing cold-calling as collaborative thinking, where the teacher positions themselves as a fellow thinker and the student as a competent contributor, produces extended, thoughtful responses; framing it instead as a moral obligation to participate, with the teacher as a task-setting authority simply waiting for compliance, produces hesitant, minimal ones. The post-phase — how the student reacts and how the teacher responds to that reaction — is identified as the crucial diagnostic window for judging whether a given cold-call actually worked. Barton's implication is that cold-calling is not a single technique with a fixed effect; its success rides almost entirely on the framing and body language surrounding the moment a name is called.
points: Cold-calling is reframed as a three-phase interactional sequence (preparation, the call itself, and the post-phase response) rather than a single moment of naming a student — each phase is a separate lever a teacher can get right or wrong.

Embodied, nonverbal cues — posture, gaze, facial expression, gesture — are shown to carry as much weight as the words used, meaning training on cold-calling that focuses only on scripts misses half of what actually shapes the student's experience.

Framing cold-calling as collaborative thinking (teacher as fellow thinker, student as competent contributor) produced extended, thoughtful responses, while framing it as moral obligation (teacher as authority awaiting compliance) produced hesitant, minimal ones — the same technique, opposite outcomes, purely from framing.
The post-phase — how the teacher responds to the student's answer — is flagged as the crucial diagnostic moment for judging whether a cold-call actually built engagement or shut it down.

The study's own framing of cold-calling as “ambivalent” — capable of being both encouraging and confrontational — cautions against treating it as a uniformly safe or uniformly risky technique; the framing determines which it becomes.
quotes: This research article examines how teachers engage “silent” students in classroom discussions, specifically focusing on the technique of cold-calling. The authors argue that while cold-calling can be an effective engagement strategy, it can also be perceived as a face-threat, and the way in which teachers enact cold-calling plays a crucial role in its reception by students.

Cold-calling is a complex, sequentially organized practice that involves more than just nominating a student. It includes a preparation phase where the teacher sets up a participation framework, the actual cold-calling with a direct address and individual task, and a post-phase where the student reacts and the teacher responds.
Embodied resources like posture, gaze, facial expressions, and gestures play a significant role in framing the activity and conveying expectations.

One approach is to frame the activity as collaborative thinking, where the teacher acts as a fellow thinker and assigns challenging tasks that encourage students to think critically and engage in discussion. This approach positions students as competent and cooperative learners and can facilitate meaningful contributions to the learning process.

Another approach frames participation as a moral obligation, emphasizing diligence, courage, and participation as social norms. The teacher acts as a task-setting authority, observing and waiting for students to comply.
Cold-calling is an ambivalent practice that can be encouraging and engaging on the one hand, but also confrontational and intimidating on the other hand
